# Computing statistics









Computing population genetic statistics requires a specification of _what_
should be computed and _how_. Which individuals should a computation be
performed on? If multiple individuals should be grouped together, how do we
define these groups?

This chapter will teach you how to do this with _slendr_ by guiding you through
exercises focused on the most fundamental concepts of population genomics. The
focus will be less on teaching you how these concepts work (after all, you might
be already be quite familiar with population genetics from your studies or work)
and more to give you the opportunity to learn the technicalities of R and
_slendr_ in a familiar context.

That said, I have designed the exercises to provide interesting puzzles to
showcase the usefulness of simulation-based exploration even in (seemingly)
basic scenarios and applications, so that even readers relatively well familiar
with population genomics will appreciate a new perspective on familiar topics.
Every single one of them represents a question I myself had, and my solutions
are the means I used myself to get the answers.











## Preparation


**Let's start with the following single-population model to keep things as
simple as possible. Look through the code to understand what it does, then save
it as `slendr_statistics.R`. Run the entire script and inspect the
produced visualization to make sure your understanding is correct.**

```{r}
#| output: false
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)

model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

plot_model(model)

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

samples <- ts_names(ts)
```












## Exercise: Adding mutations

When you typed `ts` in your R console earlier, you may have noticed a strange
thing --- although `msprime()` simulated genomic data, there are no mutations!
How can this be?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### See the `ts` summary

Here's the summary of the `ts` object simulated from the script above---notice
the "Mutations" field in the table below:

```{r}
ts
```

:::

As we will see later, the magic of tree sequences allows us to compute any
population genetic statistic without mutations. That said, particularly for
exploring statistics computed by various third-party software outside of R,
having mutations is often useful. Here's how we can make that happen.

---

**Modify the part of your script `slendr_statistics.R` by "piping" the
output of the `msprime()` function to `ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)`
(remember the `%>%` "pipe operator" introduced in the earlier chapters). After
you execute this new command and type `ts` in the R console to inspect the
summary, you should see that mutations have been added.**
  
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's the general pattern of how we simulate genomic data with _slendr_
including mutations:
  
```{r}
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

We can see that, indeed, the tree sequence now has `{r} ts$num_mutations`
mutations in it:
  
```{r}
ts
```

:::

Even though mutations are generally not needed, there's almost never any huge
downside to adding them, so I recommend you always use both `msprime()` and
`ts_mutate()` in your models.








---







With that out of the way, let's proceed with computing population genetic
statistics using _slendr_ and _tskit_.




## Exercise: Within-group(s) statistics --- nucleotide diversity

The simplest possible computation we can do is to compute a statistic from a
single population. As an example, let's look at [nucleotide diversity
$\pi$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity), implemented by a
_slendr_ function `ts_diversity()`.

If you **look at its help page under `?ts_diversity`**, you will see that it
accepts several arguments---for now let's focus on the first two, `ts =` (which
is obviously a tree-sequence object, such as the one produced by the `msprime()`
engine) and `sample_sets =`.

---

**Compute `ts_diversity()` on a single simulated individual, such as the
individual with the name "pop_1". Knowing that _slendr_ simulates diploids and
knowing the definition of [nucleotide
diversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity), how would you
interpret the result?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

The answer is that we get that individual's heterozygosity---the proportion of
their genome (two chromosomes, because each individual is diploid) carrying
heterozygous sites:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")
```

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- sum((ts_genotypes(ts)[, c("pop_1_chr1", "pop_1_chr2")] %>% rowSums()) == 1) / ts$sequence_length -->
<!-- ``` -->

Note that this is the same thing as the following command:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1"))
```

This is because in R, a single value is the same thing as a vector of length one
(this might seem like a bit of curious R trivia but it's good to keep in mind):

```{r}
"single_value" == c("single_value")

length(c("single_value"))
length("single_value")
```

:::

---

**Now run the following three commands. They look extremely similar, right? Do
they produce the same value? If not, can you decipher a general rule from the
results obtained how _slendr_ interprets these?**

```{r}
#| output: false
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
```

It turns out that patterns like these are very important for computing any kind
of tree-sequence statistic with _slendr_, so it very much pays off to think
about this, even though this looks trivial and nit-picky!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

The first command is supposed to demonstrate that specifying a vector of
individuals' names to a statistic which operates within a given group of samples
simply computes that statistic as if each individual was its own sample:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2"))
```

The second command features the same vector of names, but wrapped in `list()`.
This is how you can instruct _slendr_ to treat a given set of individuals as
a group---and in this case, compute a statistic for the group as a whole. In this
context, this command computes the nucleotide diversity within the given sample
of two individuals from the whole population "pop":

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))
```

Notice that _slendr_ assigned this "anonymous" group of individuals the name "set_1".
Because these default names can be confusing in more complex computations of more
complex statistics, you can optionally specify the name of your group by providing
the set of individuals as a named list instead (see the R bootcamp chapter in case
you need a refresher on named lists and similar topics):

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))
```

:::


---

Of course, you can compute any statistic not only for one group of individuals,
but for multiple of them. What result such computation produces depends on
whether we're computing so-called ["one-way"](https://tskit.dev/tskit/docs/stable/stats.html#sec-stats-sample-sets-one-way)
statistics (which are computed within groups, like nucleotide diversity here) or ["multi-way"](https://tskit.dev/tskit/docs/stable/stats.html#multi-way-methods)
statistic (which are computed between groups, like $F_{ST}$). For now we'll stay with 
one-way statistics.

**To make the "one-way" statistic concept clear, let's practice this. Instead of
computing `ts_diversity()` for a single group of individuals (like "pop_1" and
"pop_2" above), compute this using a single `ts_diversity()` command on multiple
subsets of individuals of increasing sizes (let's say groups of 1, 2, 5, 10, 500
1000, and finally all individuals). Do you expect the same value of nucleotide
diversity? And why?**

**Hint:** You can get a random subset of a larger set of elements using the
built-in R function `sample()`. Take a look at `?sample` manual page if you need
more help.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's first generate the subsets of individuals of different sizes. We have
a number of options:

1. We could do it "manually" like this:

```{r}
# first get all names of all individuals recorded in the tree sequence
all_inds <- ts_names(ts)

# then manually create all subset names
subsets <- list(
  sample(all_inds, 1),
  sample(all_inds, 2),
  sample(all_inds, 5),
  sample(all_inds, 10),
  sample(all_inds, 500),
  sample(all_inds, 1000),
  all_inds
)
```

2. Alternatively, we could do it more succinctly using this R pattern:

```{r}
# first get the desired sizes of all subsets
sizes <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 500, 1000, length(all_inds))

# then iterate over those sizes, and applying the sample() function to each
subsets <- lapply(sizes, sample, x = all_inds)
# let's also add names to the groups based on their sizes, for easier reference
names(subsets) <- sizes
```

Either way, these commands give us a list of vector of appropriate lengths,
which we can verify like this. It's very useful to do these sanity checks as
your working on your programs, always making sure that what you want to do
_actually_ matches reality:

```{r}
# apple the length() function to each element of the list
sapply(subsets, length)
```

Now we can finally compute nucleotide diversity in each of those groups of
individuals:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, subsets)
```

Perhaps not surprisingly, we don't see much difference. After all, this is
expected, because there is only one true (and normally unknown) value of
nucleotide diversity of the entire population. What changes when we compute this
statistic on subsets of different sizes is the stochastic noise.

We'll see a bit more on how to control (and quantify) the noise using simulations
a little bit later.

:::










## Exercise: Parameter estimation --- $N_e$

In practical research, we often use various software or statistics to estimate
some parameter of interest. In our context---again, to use a very simple toy
example to demonstrate a simulation-based approach in a familiar context---let's
look at a measure of the population size called [effective population
size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_population_size), or $N_e$.

From a bit of [background theory of population
genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_population_size#Empirical_measurements),
we know that we can obtain an estimate of $N_e$ from nucleotide diversity (which
we just computed). Specifically, neutral theory of molecular evolution posits
that an idealised diploid population will have a pairwise nucleotide diversity
equal to

$$\theta = 4 N_e \mu,$$

where $\mu$ is the mutation rate. Using simple algebra to rearrange this
equation, this gives us an estimate for $N_e$ in the form of

$$N_e = \frac{\theta}{4 \mu}.$$

**Let's build a simple simulation-based analysis to determine how well does this
estimator perform under different scenarios.**

::: aside

If you're familiar with population genetics, this has all sorts of obvious
answers, but let's demonstrate how we can benchmark this using simulations,
hopefully establishing a useful _slendr_ recipe which you will be able to use
very often in all kinds of contexts (some of the more complex ones will be
demonstrated later in this workshop).

:::
 
---

**Start by computing the nucleotide diversity value for every single individual
in your tree sequence and storing the result in a data frame `df`. Then, use the
equation above to estimate $N_e$ from nucleotide diversity, and add a new column
`Ne_estimated` to this data frame with this value. Do you get a reasonable
result?**

**Hint:** Remember that you know the true $N_e$ in your model --- it's the `N`
value in your simulation script! That's the most powerful thing about
simulations --- they allow you to establish a ground truth, and benchmark
various methods against it!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's get the data frame with the value of $\pi$ first:

```{r}
df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
df
```

Then add the inferred $N_e$ according to the equation above:

```{r}
df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
df
```

:::

Of course, benchmarking any method based on a single simulation of a single
number doesn't make sense --- so now let's now take things one step forward.









## Exercise: Generalizing the simulation

Suppose we need to evaluate how our hypothetical statistic of interest (in this
example, the estimator of $N_e$) behaves under different parameters, different,
models, different bioinformatic processing, etc.

To do this, we could make a copy of our original script, modify it a bunch of
times, and re-run the modifications as needed, collecting the results in the
process. This works, but is almost always the wrong approach. The correct way to
do this is to generalize our code into a self-contained function.

To demonstrate, let's break this down into individual steps (in software
engineering, this process of modifying code and improving it is called
["refactoring"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_refactoring)).

---

**First, create and save a new script called `slendr_Ne_pi.R`. We'll be
working on our improvements in this new file.**

---

**In this script, create a function called `sim_constant`, which will accept a
single argument `Ne_true`, and will "wrap around" the following bits of code (in
other words, copy-pasting what you programmed in the original
`slendr_statistics.R` and wrapping it into a function):**

1. **the code implementing our _slendr_ demographic `model`**,

2. **the command simulating a `ts` object from the `model`**,

3. **the commands creating the `df` data frame with nucleotide diversity,**

4. **the computation of `Ne_estimated` from nucleotide diversity,**

5. **adding a column to `df` called `Ne_true` and assigning it the `Ne_true`
argument of your function.**

6. **Your function should return this `df` object as its output.**

**When you're done, all the code doing the above should be gone from your script,
entirely replaced by this function.**

**Hint:** If you need help, you can use the following template which shows how
should your script look like when you're done.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(model) {
  # move the bits of code doing 1.-6. inside this function

  # write the bits of code to do 5. and 6. afterwards

  # finally, return the df data frame like this
  return(df)
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's how my entire `slendr_statistics_Ne.R` looks like:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}
```

:::

---

**To test your function, restart your R session (in RStudio go to `Session ->
Restart R`), then run your entire script. Then, evaluate your function in the R
console by running it for different values of $N_e$ (for instance, type
`sim_constant(100)`, sim_constant(1234)`, `sim_constant(20000)`, etc.). Each of
your function calls should produce a data frame with the appropriate value of
$\pi$ and the estimated $N_e$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's what I get with my implementation:

```{r}
sim_constant(Ne_true = 100)
sim_constant(Ne_true = 1234)
sim_constant(Ne_true = 20000)
```

:::

---

Doing all this extra programming work might seem like unnecessary bother. In
fact, it looks like we've so far written _even more code_! But the pay off comes
later, as you will see.

Custom functions are absolutely critical for efficient, reproducible science.
They eliminate copy-pasted bug-prone code and make it much easier to explore
ideas, test parameters, and explore various models. In this workshop, I'll be
often forcing you to write custom functions---hopefully, by the end you will
appreciate why I did this!










## Exercise: Simulations across parameter grids

Whenever we want to benchmark a statistic, or understand its expected behavior
under different circumstances, we often need to re-run a model many times,
usually for different model parameters (or different models entirely).

**Imagine we want to compute our inference on many different potential values of
true $N_e$**, what we could do is something like the exercise above, running the
model individually. But this isn't very scalable, definitely whenever we want to
run the same model across a huge number of parameter values (or even multiple
such parameters).

In cases like this, **we want to is to use "looping", such as the function
`map_dfr()` from the package _purrr_**:

Imagine a function like this, which creates a data frame of a value and its
square:

```{r}
silly_fun <- function(x) {
  data.frame(value = x, squared = x * x)
}
```

The way we use `map_dfr` is by providing a list of values of our parameter of
interest, and a function name. In the case of our silly function, we can use it
like this:

```{r}
library(purrr)

map_dfr(c(100, 1234, 20000), silly_fun)
```

The name `map_dfr` stands for _"`map` a given function producing a `d`ata
`f`rame and then bind its `r`ows together, hence, `map_dfr`. When you look at
its output above, this is exactly what happened.

---

**In your script `slendr_statistics_Ne.R`, program a simulation of $N_e$
inference across the grid of `Ne_true` values of `c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000,
5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)`, then visualize the results as a scatterplot of
`Ne_true` against `Ne_estimated`. Use the function `purrr::map_dfr()` to do this
efficiently.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)

ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")
```

:::

---


This toy exercise is a great example of how to use these kinds of simulations in
practice. Again, nucleotide diverisity-based $N_e$ estimation and its
benchmarking across a range of parameters really is a toy example, but this idea
extends to many other settings:

- benchmarking of IBD accuracy across different gene-flow scenarios

- validating  qpAdm inference results for various possible admixture graphs

- testing the robustness of local ancestry inference methods (LAI) and admixture dating inference as a function of admixture times and proportions

- understanding how PCA differs for different sample sizes from different populations

... and many others. All of this is something that I do in my daily work (and
something that almost any paper in population genomics should be doing to
validate their results).







## Exercise: Comparing multiple models

Let's make it a bit more interesting. Suppose we want to see how robust our
statistic of interest is to the underlying demographic model (which is almost
always uncertain).

In the previous exercise, we worked with using $\pi$ to estimate the $N_e$ a
population under study ($N_e$) and verified that it works very well for a model
of a long-term constant population size.

But what about population that experienced a resize event? How well does our
$N_e$ estimate work in such case?

---

**In your script `slendr_statistics_Ne.R`, make a copy of your function
`sim_constant()` named `sim_resize()`. Make the following changes in this
function:**

1. **the population "pop" will start with $N_e$ of 5000,**

2. **the population will experience a population resize (implemented by the
function `resize()`), which will set the size of the population to the function
argument `Ne_true` at time 500.**

**Then, use the function `map_dfr()` to run the new function `sim_resize()`
along the same parameter grid as before, again visualizing the results of
`Ne_true` against `Ne_estimated`. How well does our diversity-based $N_e$
estimate perform in such a demographic scenario? Is it robust to non-constant
demographic histories? If not, why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the solution---new function `sim_resize()`, new simulation run against a
parameter grid, and a visualization of results:

```{r}
# new function to simulate population size change
sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# simulations across a parameter grid
Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)

# visualization of results
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)
```

We can see that even a large population resize event doesn't change the observed
levels of nucleotide diversity that much. As a result, the $N_e$ based on the
population nucleotide diversity parameter $\theta$ is very wrong---we
consistently estimate it at the level of 5000 (i.e., the size prior to the
bottleneck), regardless of the true size of the population after the bottleneck.

:::








## Exercise: Expanding the parameter grid

Our hypothesis for how poorly the nucleotide diversity-based estimate is doing
under non-constant population size is the fact that the resize event was very
recent. As a result, diversity hasn't yet reached an equilibrium value.

Let's test this hypothesis while, at the same time, showing how we can expand
the parameter grid simulations to include another parameter---this time the time
of the population size change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the solution.

First, the new function `sim_resize()`

```{r}
sim_change <- function(Ne_true, T_change) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = T_change)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  df$T_change <- T_change
  
  df
}
```

A new simulation run against a parameter grid:

```{r}
Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- rbind(
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1),    # change 1 generation ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 100),  # change 100 generations ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1000), # etc.
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 2000)
)
```

And finally, visualization of results:

```{r}
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)",
          subtitle = "Each panel indicates the time of the population size change") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000) +
  facet_wrap(~ T_change)
```

We can see that, indeed, the older the population resize event, the more time
there's for the population to either lose the variation (in case of a
bottleneck), or gain new variation (in case of population size increase), which
means that the $N_e$ estimated based on the $\theta = 4 N_e \mu$ nucleotide
diversity parameter is going to be close to the true (unknown) population size.

:::

---

In the case of this example, the problem with the nucleotide diversity is that
it effectively reduces the entirety of genetic variation in the population
(which mutations there are at which frequencies) into a single  number.
As a result, we lose a lot of potentially very useful information about the
population's demographic history. When we try to estimate $N_e$ using this
summary statistic, we can only hope to infer a long-term $N_e$.

As we've seen, a single bottleneck doesn't cause nucleotide diversity to drop
significantly enough for us to pick up that this bottleneck even happened.




## Exercise: Allele frequency spectrum (AFS)

**Create a new script called `slendr_Ne_afs.R`. Copy-paste the following code
into that script. Note that this is the same exact model we started this section
(except for the one line which selects only 20 individuals from all individuals
recorded in the tree sequence).**

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)
model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
```

---

Unlike nucleotide diversity which, as mentioned above, reduces the entire
genomic variation of a population into a single number, the [allele frequency
spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allele_frequency_spectrum) carries
information about the distribution of the counts of mutations at each observable
frequency.

**Look at the `?ts_afs` help page to learn how the _slendr_ function `ts_afs()`
works. As you've seen, `ts_diversity()` (like the vast majority of _slendr_
statistical functions) produces a data frame. What data format does `ts_afs()`
produce? Compute the AFS from your simulated tree sequence `ts` on your `subset`
of individuals, then visualize it (with whatever means you know).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

As we can see, `ts_afs()` produces a plain R vector of integer numbers, each of
which represents the count of mutations observed at a given frequency --- the
count of singletons, the count of doubletons, etc.:

```{r}
afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
afs
```

This vector can be easily visualized with a base-R function `plot()`:

```{r}
plot(afs, type = "l", col = "lightblue", xlab = "allele frequency", ylab = "count")
```

:::

---

But does the AFS really carry more information about demographic changes?

**Write a new function in your script, called `sim_afs()`, which will again
accept a single argument `Ne_true` and implement the exact same demographic
model as you did in your function `sim_change()` (i.e., resize from the initial
`N` of 5000 to the given value of `Ne_true` at time 1000). In this function,
compute the `afs` vector from this model, then run it for a range of `Ne_true`
values and visualize the individual AFS results. Does AFS pick up signal even
from such recent population size changes?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's a function which simulates an AFS for a demographic history given by the
`Ne_true` argument:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 100)

  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}
```


```{r}
df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)
```

```{r}
ggplot(df_bottleneck, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")
```

For easier comparison, here are the AFS result side-by-side with the
values of nucleotide diversity from the same demographic scenarios:

```{r}
#| echo: false
cowplot::plot_grid(
  ggplot(df_bottleneck, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
    geom_line() +
    ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models"),
  ggplot(dplyr::filter(df_change, T_change == 100), aes(Ne_true, diversity)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
    xlim(0, 20000) +
    facet_wrap(~ T_change),
  nrow = 2
)
```


This simulation indicates that AFS does, indeed, carry much more information
about population history, even for recent changes in population size.

For now we'll leave this be, but towards the end of the workshop, we're going to
work through a small case-study which will demonstrate how to do
simulation-based inference by extending our toy example of $N_e$ estimation
towards a more real-world scenario.

## Bonus exercise: Your own model

If you got all the way here while the others are still working on their solutions,
here's a bonus exercise for you.

**Take a demographic model of an organism or a population which is of your
interest in your own research (either your own model or a model you know from
the literature) and program it with _slendr_. Feel free to be as detailed (or
not) as possible, but don't worry about accuracy of various parameters. The
point is to practice building a model from scratch. Then, compute the basic
summary statistics introduced in this chapter on simulations from your model. Do
the results match what you know, either from your research or from the
literature? If not, what could be the problem?**

If these statistics aren't particularly interesting or relevant for your
research, don't despair. Again, the point is to practice, but even then, you'll
have plenty of opportunities to compute more interesting things throughout this
course, particularly during the "freeform" sessions at the very end.
